title: Russia Expands Power to Seize Property of Citizens Abroad Under Sweeping New Law
excerpt: Federal Law 168-FZ, signed by Putin and taking effect September 1, vastly broadens extraterritorial prosecution of Russians overseas, enabling courts to freeze bank accounts and seize property without the accused being present or even notified.
body:
• Russia's new law expands extraterritorial administrative offenses from 4 to 16 categories, targeting dissent abroad including "discrediting" the military, calling for sanctions, and insulting government officials.
  • Courts can seize property and freeze bank accounts of Russians abroad as a precautionary measure — with no requirement that seized assets match the fine amount.
  • Property arrests can be ordered before the underlying case is heard, without notifying the accused, and decisions take immediate legal effect with no appeal period.
  • The law takes effect September 1, 2026, and applies to Russian citizens, foreign nationals, stateless persons, and foreign legal entities.

A New Legal Arsenal Against Dissent Abroad

Russian President Vladimir Putin has signed Federal Law No. 168-FZ, a sweeping amendment to Russia's Code on Administrative Offenses that dramatically expands Moscow's ability to prosecute and financially punish its citizens living abroad. Approved by the Federation Council on June 3 and signed into law on June 10, the legislation takes effect on September 1, 2026.

https://x.com/alex_kokcharov/status/2084684125852590241

"In May 2026, Putin signed a separate law authorizing the Russian armed forces to protect Russian citizens who are "arrested, detained or otherwise prosecuted" by foreign courts, according to Xinhua."

The law quadruples the list of administrative offenses subject to extraterritorial jurisdiction — from four to 16 — according to an analysis by the International Center for Not-for-Profit Law (ICNL). The newly covered offenses include insulting the head of state, "discrediting" the Russian Armed Forces, calling for international sanctions against Russia, producing or disseminating materials deemed "extremist," and publicly comparing the Soviet Union's leadership to Nazi Germany.

Property Seizure Without Limits

The most consequential provision introduces a broad mechanism for the arrest of property. Under a rewritten Article 27.20 of the Code on Administrative Offenses, Russian courts can freeze bank accounts, apartments, business shares, vehicles, and other assets held within Russia by persons located abroad, according to ICNL.

Critically, there is no cap linking seized assets to the fine amount. As Meduza reported, "the value of seized property may be disproportionate to the fine itself." The law prioritizes freezing money held in bank accounts and deposits first; if insufficient funds are found, other property can be arrested.

Courts can order these seizures before even hearing the underlying administrative case, at the request of a prosecutor, the Ministry of Justice, or tax authorities. Judges must rule on seizure motions within one day — and can do so without notifying the accused.

Formalizing an Existing Crackdown

While Russian courts had previously fined people located outside the country under administrative statutes, the seizure of property as a precautionary measure had not been legally provided for, according to Meduza. The law formalizes and dramatically strengthens what had been an ad hoc practice.

The legislation also strips away procedural protections. Administrative penalty decisions now take legal effect from the day they are issued, eliminating the standard appeal period. Defense counsel is appointed for absent defendants, but the costs — including travel, accommodation, and per diem expenses — are charged to the accused.

Russian experts cited by ICNL believe the new measures are designed to silence vocal exiles. The law's broad formulation of covered conduct and the undefined reference to acts "directed against the interests of the Russian Federation" create substantial uncertainty for anyone outside Russia who retains assets within its jurisdiction.

Part of a Broader Pattern

The law arrives amid an accelerating campaign to extend Moscow's legal reach beyond its borders. In May 2026, Putin signed a separate law authorizing the Russian armed forces to protect Russian citizens who are "arrested, detained or otherwise prosecuted" by foreign courts, according to Xinhua. State Duma Chairman Vyacheslav Volodin argued the law was necessary because "Western justice has turned into a repressive machine."

In December 2025, Putin signed legislation giving Russia the formal right to ignore criminal judgments issued by foreign and international courts without Moscow's participation, as Reuters reported. That move came as the International Criminal Court, Ukraine, and European bodies pursued accountability for alleged Russian war crimes.

Meanwhile, Amnesty International documented in January 2026 how Russia's Federal Security Service initiated criminal proceedings against prominent exiled opposition figures, including members of the Anti-War Committee of Russia. Charges of "violent seizure of power" and "organization of a terrorist community" were brought in absentia against 23 members, including former prisoner of conscience Vladimir Kara-Murza and ex-Prime Minister Mikhail Kasyanov.

Impact on the Diaspora

For members of the Russian-speaking diaspora — including those in India and across South Asia — the law raises immediate practical questions. Russians who emigrated after the 2022 invasion and still hold property, bank accounts, or business interests in Russia face the prospect of those assets being frozen over a social media post or a public statement deemed offensive to the state.

The ICNL analysis notes that even Russians with no assets in Russia may face consequences: unpaid administrative fines remain on record and can block access to consular services abroad, including passport renewals and notarized documents.

The legislation also extends liability to foreign citizens and legal entities for offenses committed outside Russia, a provision particularly relevant for businesses and individuals with cross-border ties.

What Comes Next

With the law taking effect on September 1, the coming weeks will test how aggressively Russian authorities deploy these new tools. The State Duma is separately advancing legislation to confiscate assets of individuals convicted of inciting "extremist" activities and advocating for sanctions, as reported by the Organized Crime and Corruption Reporting Project (OCCRP). Duma Speaker Volodin has framed the effort as targeting those who "live comfortable lives" abroad while undermining the Russian state.

For the estimated hundreds of thousands of Russians who left the country since 2022, the message is stark: distance from Moscow no longer guarantees distance from its legal system.
